extracted.intended_audience: general readers, television critics, fans of comedy/docu-comedy, media scholars
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting criteria one might use to evaluate or produce a docu-comedy television series like The Rehearsal—covering premise, production design, ethics, tone, thematic depth, representation, and craft (editing, acting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise / Concept: rehearsal-based simulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The central conceit is helping ordinary people rehearse difficult conversations or life events by building sets and hiring actors to recreate real situations and run dialogue trees dozens of times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the page: trivial rehearsals (confessing a lie about education) to complex ones (raising a child); information used to train actors and build sets is often collected without subjects' knowledge — an element played for comedic effect. Evaluate clarity, originality, and feasibility of the conceit and how well episodes realize it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production design / fidelity of sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagant, meticulously detailed sets are a major source of the show's humour and storytelling—full-scale replicas of bars, houses, and even an airport terminal are constructed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page details: replica of the Alligator Lounge bar, duplicate house, and a large-scale replica of George Bush Intercontinental Airport with lounges, restaurants, signage, and staff areas. Assess fidelity, attention to detail, and how set design enables repeated rehearsals and narrative beats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actor training / the 'Fielder Method' realism
rubrics_metrics.description: A production-specific acting approach involving covertly observing and imitating unaware subjects, immersive role-play, and actors deeply inhabiting simulated lives to produce believable rehearsals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes Nathan opening an acting studio teaching the Fielder Method, recruiting actors, immersion tactics (actors living in others' homes), and using graduates to portray emergency responders, family members, etc. Consider casting choices, actor preparation, believability, and consequences for performers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone balance: comedy vs. sincerity / ethical stance
rubrics_metrics.description: How well the series balances absurdist/comedic aims with sincere, sometimes serious ambitions (e.g., improving real-world outcomes) and handles the ethical implications of manipulating real people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Season-two material highlights tension between 'somewhat sincere' efforts (pilot safety) and expectations of a comedy show; critics debate the show's disingenuousness and 'cruel and arrogant gaze.' Evaluate whether tone shifts feel coherent or exploitative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedic style / absurdist and deadpan execution
rubrics_metrics.description: The show's humor is described as absurdist and delivered with deadpan aplomb, pushing its conceit to extreme, uncomfortable places.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rotten Tomatoes critics consensus: the series 'gives Nathan Fielder carte blanche to take his absurdist comedy to the limit' with deadpan delivery. Assess consistency of comedic voice, risk-taking, and audience reception of cringe/awkward humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thematic and philosophical depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the series has a deeper philosophical core — e.g., interrogating whether it's possible to truly understand another person — beyond its comedic premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NYT and Vox reviews cited the show's exploration of understanding others and comparisons to literature/philosophy. Evaluate presence and integration of themes, whether thematic ambitions are realized or merely provocative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blurring of simulation and reality / meta-textuality
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the series intentionally blurs enacted simulations and real life, producing meta-commentary and making viewers question authenticity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article compares the show to Synecdoche, New York and Remainder; it repeatedly repurposes sets and actors to collapse boundaries. Evaluate clarity and effect of this blurring on narrative and ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical treatment of participants (including children)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the production treats non-actor participants and vulnerable people (children, neurodivergent participants), including consent, psychological impact, and legal/child-protection constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Episodes described: covertly switching a baby every four hours due to child protection laws, child actors becoming attached to Nathan, and scenes provoking real emotional harm. Assess informed consent practices, safeguards, and whether ethical concerns are acknowledged or exploited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation and resonance with neurodivergent audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the show's choices and central conceit resonate with or represent autistic/neurodivergent experiences (e.g., masking) and how responsibly that resonance is handled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page notes many autistic viewers viewed the show as an analogy for masking and that season-two engaged with autistic experience. Evaluate sensitivity, accuracy, and the show's impact on neurodivergent viewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing and narrative construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of editing in shaping the final product, controlling tone, pacing, and the apparent ethics/truth of events presented on-screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: External commentary linked: 'Why The Rehearsal's Editing Is So Important to the Final Product' (Slate). Consider how editing choices create narrative arcs, comedic timing, and the portrayal of participants and events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk-taking / boundary-pushing as a creative choice
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent to which the series intentionally pushes social and ethical boundaries (putting people in embarrassing or emotionally fraught situations) as part of its artistic practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vulture highlighted Fielder's 'willingness to screw with people'; some critics praise boldness while others call it cruel. Assess whether risk-taking produces insight/art or gratuitous harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Real‑world impact / practical application of simulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the show's simulations aim for or achieve measurable real-world benefits (e.g., improving pilot communication, informing hearings) versus serving purely as entertainment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Season-two arcs involve role-play simulation proposed for pilot safety and a Congressional Subcommittee hearing; evaluate evidence of genuine impact, engagement with experts, and the legitimacy of practical claims.
